method: An IPv4 multicast group (224.0.0.0/4) maps to the Ethernet MAC 01:00:5e followed by the low 23 bits of the group address (RFC 1112), so bits 27 to 23 are dropped and 32 groups share one MAC; the fourth MAC octet can only reach 7f, so a 01:00:5e address whose fourth octet is 80 to ff has no IPv4 group. An IPv6 multicast group (ff00::/8) maps to 33:33 followed by the low 32 bits (RFC 2464), so 96 bits are dropped and 2^96 groups share one MAC. The page accepts an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address (any valid group syntax, an optional %zone id, a dotted IPv4 tail) or a MAC in colon, dash, Cisco dotted or bare form, checks the multicast (I/G) bit in the first octet, and refuses unicast MACs and multicast MACs outside the 01:00:5e and 33:33 prefixes. IPv4 results list all 32 groups with the same low 23 bits; IPv6 results give the low 32 bits and the link-local example group. Address blocks are labelled (224.0.0.0/24 link-local, 224.0.1.0/24 internetwork control, 232.0.0.0/8 source-specific, 233.0.0.0/8 GLOP, 239.0.0.0/8 administratively scoped) and the IPv6 scope comes from the low nibble of the second octet. The page states that a switch forwarding table cannot distinguish groups that share a MAC. Everything runs in the browser with no network access, uploads or storage.

sources.title: RFC 1112, Host Extensions for IP Multicasting (1989): IPv4 multicast groups in 224.0.0.0/4 and the Ethernet mapping to 01:00:5e plus the low 23 bits.
RFC 2464, Transmission of IPv6 Packets over Ethernet Networks (1998): the multicast MAC 33:33 followed by the low 32 bits of the IPv6 group.
RFC 4291, IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture (2006): the ff00::/8 format, its flags and scope fields, and the scope values reported here.
IEEE 802-2014, IEEE Standard for Local and Metropolitan Area Networks: the I/G bit in the first octet separates group (multicast) from individual (unicast) MAC addresses.
